You said it yourself, "when laying drops I still have to feed them the same, so I'm spending without earning," and that squeeze is happening because your biggest cost is set by the shop, not by you. **NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to work out your exact feed cost per tray, then price out mixing your own feed from local maize and silverfish so you can see how many shillings per tray you would actually save.

The spoilage comes from a commitment problem — none of her demand is locked in before she buys, so she carries all the perishability risk that could be shifted to buyers through advance orders.

The spoilage comes from a positioning problem — she is an undifferentiated seller in a crowd of identical sellers where "who the customer reaches first" decides sales, so any produce she buys may rot simply because a neighbor got the customer, not because she misjudged quantity.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** Your spoilage comes from guessing blind. You buy from the trucks very early morning before you have any idea how busy that day will be, so some days you buy plenty and the market is slow, and other days you buy little and run out. In your own words, "I can never judge how much to buy and it changes every day," which is exactly the problem of choosing without information.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the real cause, you should notice that your worst spoilage days do not follow any pattern you can explain, sometimes a heavy buy sells out, sometimes the same amount rots, and you cannot tell in the morning which kind of day it will be.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to keep a simple daily record for two weeks, writing down what you bought, what sold, and what spoiled, plus the day of the week and weather. This turns your blind guessing into a real pattern you can buy against.
